case_study_insert.main_stem: Solstice Off-grid Lighting (SOL) is a private limited company in the renewable-energy sector, employing a workforce of 30. Founded in 2016 by Amara Nwosu, the business manufactures and installs rooftop solar lighting units and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. SOL plans to invest $1,200,000 in an automated panel-assembly line, financed by an $800,000 bank loan and a $400,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $15.00 a unit and a selling price of $30.00, and currently produces 22,000 units a year. SOL faces two operational problems: a unit defect rate of 3.5% is above the industry norm and a skills gap in automated assembly is slowing output and quality.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Waste Report — Q4 2025: The assembly line produced 5,600 lighting units last quarter with a defect rate of 3.5%, down from 5.8% a year earlier. Customer complaints fell from 29 to 16 per month. Average installation time is 4.1 days. A survey of 350 installers and builders found that 60% would pay up to $1.00 more for units with a 25-year warranty, and 54% check product certification before specifying a supplier. A training needs analysis shows 9 of 30 technicians lack automated-assembly skills; on-the-job training is available, while off-the-job training at the local college costs $1,100 per technician.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Solstice Off-grid Lighting for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.25%, increasing borrowing costs on variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.7% from $13.00 to $13.87 per hour from April 2026, lifting skilled-technician wage bills. (3) Polysilicon and glass input costs rose 13.5% year-on-year, renewable-energy investment grew 9.2%, and construction activity slowed 1.8%.

questions.question_text: SOL raised $400,000 through a share issue. Explain two disadvantages for SOL of using a share issue to help fund the $1,200,000 assembly line.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A share issue gives away part of the ownership of SOL, so Amara Nwosu and existing shareholders dilute their control and must share future dividends with new investors. As the business grows on the back of the $1,200,000 line and 9.2% renewable-energy investment, a larger share of the profits would leave the company rather than being retained.

Point 2: Share issue costs and the need to satisfy new shareholders can be significant, and unlike the $800,000 bank loan there is no tax-efficient interest charge; dividends are paid from profit after tax. With fixed costs of $240,000 and a 3.5% defect rate still to fix, diverting cash to dividends reduces the money available for the $1,100 per technician training and for absorbing the 13.5% polysilicon and glass rise. Issuing shares when the share price is weak can also raise less than the $400,000 needed. With 2025 revenue of $2,500,000 in Appendix 2, the dilution must be weighed against the growth the new line should deliver.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid disadvantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to SOL and its assembly-line financing decision.

questions.question_text: SOL is promoting its new 25-year-warranty solar lighting units. Consider a national television campaign, trade-exhibition stands, or partnerships with installers and builders. Which should SOL choose to promote the product? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Television campaign: A national TV campaign would create rapid mass awareness of solar lighting, but airtime and production costs are very high and most viewers cannot install or specify the product. For a 30-employee firm servicing an $800,000 loan and facing 13.5% higher input costs, most of the spend would be wasted and few of the 350 surveyed installers would be reached.

Trade-exhibition stands: Industry exhibitions put SOL in front of technical buyers who understand certification and warranties, allowing live demonstrations of the 25-year warranty. However, stands and travel are expensive, reach is limited to those attending, and the 54% of survey respondents who check certification may still need follow-up before placing orders.

Partnerships with installers and builders: Working through the installers and builders already in the market targets exactly the 60% of 350 survey respondents willing to pay $1.00 more for a 25-year warranty, with the warranty built into the specification and measurable referral sales. The 54% who check certification can be shown the product credentials directly at low cost.

Recommendation: SOL should choose partnerships with installers and builders. This reaches the precise segment identified in the survey, costs little and turns the warranty into a selling point at the point of specification. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a firm with an $800,000 loan; trade exhibitions are rejected as expensive and narrow, though select shows can support the installer partnerships. The 4.1-day installation time can be used in joint installer material to demonstrate reliability. Installer referrals also build credibility with the 54% who check certification.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of SOL with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of SOL with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and exhibitions are rejected.

questions.question_text: SOL has a skills gap in automated assembly and uses laissez-faire leadership. Explain two benefits for SOL of introducing democratic leadership to address the skills gap and the 3.5% defect rate.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives SOL's workforce of 30 a real voice in how the new automated assembly line is organised, satisfying social and esteem needs and raising job satisfaction. Technicians who help set quality checks and assembly routines are more likely to take ownership of the 3.5% defect rate, reducing faults and the 22,000-unit output disruption caused by the current skills gap.

Point 2: Consulting technicians draws on their practical experience to solve the skills gap, generating training ideas that a laissez-faire approach might miss. Higher involvement raises commitment and reduces labour turnover, saving the $1,100 per technician training cost and protecting quality as the $1,200,000 line is installed. Better morale also supports product reliability, which matters to the 54% of surveyed builders who check certification before specifying a supplier. The defect rate has already fallen from 5.8% to 3.5%, showing that better-trained, involved technicians can improve quality as the automated line arrives.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to SOL's skills gap, defects and output.

questions.question_text: SOL must train 9 technicians to operate the new automated assembly line. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should SOL choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training at the assembly line is directly relevant to SOL's own equipment and quality standards, costs no course fees, and keeps the 9 technicians productive while they learn, protecting the 22,000-unit output and the effort to cut the 3.5% defect rate. However, trainers are working technicians whose own tasks suffer, bad habits can spread, and there is no formal certificate if builders ask for evidence of competence.

Off-the-job training: A college course at $1,100 per technician gives structured technical knowledge and a recognised certificate for all 9, costing $9,900 in total — small against the $1,200,000 assembly line. It removes staff from production, cutting short-term capacity, and generic content may not match SOL's exact machines, so factory follow-up would still be needed.

Decision: SOL should choose on-the-job training for the initial rollout, backed by short college modules for senior technicians. It is cheapest, machine-specific and avoids further capacity loss while the skills gap persists; full off-the-job training is rejected because paying $9,900 and releasing 9 technicians would slow output and risk the 3.5% defect target, and college qualifications can be added once the automated line is running reliably. With 5,600 units produced last quarter and a 3.5% defect rate still to reduce, taking nine technicians off the line would slow output and risk quality. On-the-job training keeps production running, and the $9,900 saved could fund short certified modules once the automated line is stable. Senior technicians can then coach the remaining colleagues, keeping the 4.1-day installation time intact and supporting the 25-year warranty promise.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to SOL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of SOL.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of SOL with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how SOL's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $240,000 ÷ ($30.00 − $15.00) = $240,000 ÷ $15.00 = 16,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 16,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $30.00 − $15.00 = $15.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $15.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways SOL's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing the 16,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 22,000 units gives a margin of safety of 6,000 units, confirming the solar operation is profitable but with modest headroom, so the $1,200,000 line needs steady demand.
2. Contribution per unit of $15.00 lets managers model the $1.00 warranty premium from the survey: if offered as a discount instead, contribution would fall to $14.00 and break-even would rise to about 17,143 units ($240,000 ÷ $14.00), so volume must compensate.
3. With fixed costs of $240,000, managers can set the volume needed to service the $800,000 bank loan and check that 22,000 units covers it before further borrowing.
4. Unit cost data ($240,000 ÷ 22,000 units + $15.00 = $25.91 a unit) can be benchmarked monthly to detect the 3.5% defect rate and to judge whether the 13.5% polysilicon and glass rise is being absorbed without cutting contribution.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 16,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $15.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 6,000 units against 22,000 output; discount modelling with $1.00 and $14.00 contribution; loan servicing against $240,000 fixed costs; and unit-cost benchmarking at $25.91 to tackle the defect rate.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate the profitability of SOL by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and return on capital employed (ROCE) for 2024 and 2025. Has SOL's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.5%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 20.0%
ROCE 2025 = 25.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit of $800,000 on revenue of $2,000,000 compares with 2025 gross profit of $1,125,000 on revenue of $2,500,000; cost of sales rose only from $1,200,000 to $1,375,000 while revenue grew faster. Operating profit increased from $250,000 to $375,000, and capital employed from $1,250,000 to $1,500,000; interest payable rose from $40,000 to $60,000 but stays modest.

Evaluation: All three measures show clear improvement. The 40.0% to 45.0% change means SOL kept more of each revenue dollar after direct production costs, so the 13.5% polysilicon and glass shock was partly passed on through the $30.00 price. The 12.5% to 15.0% operating result shows overhead control as renewable-energy investment grew 9.2%, and the 20.0% to 25.0% return on capital employed shows the asset base generated substantially more operating profit even while the $1,200,000 line was funded. Interest payable remains small relative to operating profit, so the $800,000 loan is manageable. The main caution is that construction activity slowed 1.8%, which could limit future sales, and the 3.5% defect rate must be cut.

Conclusion: SOL's financial performance has improved. Gross margin, operating margin and return on capital employed all rose together between 2024 and 2025, showing broad-based progress rather than a one-off gain. SOL should proceed with the $1,200,000 investment while monitoring that the new capital earns comparable returns and that quality and the skills gap are addressed.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates all three profitability ratios for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of margins, operating profit and capital employed and a justified conclusion on whether performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for SOL of offering a 25-year warranty on its solar lighting units.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey of 350 installers and builders found 60% would pay up to $1.00 more for units with a 25-year warranty, so SOL can add a premium that protects its $15.00 contribution per unit while polysilicon and glass costs rise 13.5%. It also attracts the 54% who check certification, helping win specifications and the volume needed to justify the $1,200,000 assembly line.

Disadvantage: A 25-year warranty creates a long-term repair and replacement liability that could raise the $240,000 fixed costs if the 3.5% defect rate persists, and it requires cash reserves for future claims. With an $800,000 loan to service and a skills gap in automated assembly, SOL has little spare capacity to honour a long warranty; faulty units would also damage the certification credentials that 54% of buyers check. The slowing 1.8% construction activity also makes a 25-year warranty riskier if sales volumes fall. A 25-year warranty also commits SOL to service and replace units long after the original sale.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to SOL's survey data, costs and investment.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.7% minimum wage increase and the 13.5% rise in polysilicon and glass input costs will affect SOL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.25%): If SOL's $800,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 1.00% of $800,000 = $8,000 a year (0.01 × $800,000). That is small beside fixed costs of $240,000, and if the loan is fixed-rate the increase is zero. Higher rates may also slow the 9.2% renewable-energy investment and raise future borrowing costs, but SOL can largely remove this risk by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.7%, to $13.87 per hour): SOL employs a workforce of 30, with technicians likely paid hourly, so a wage rise feeds into its cost base and is not optional. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no defensible annual wage total can be invented; the honest test is productivity — 22,000 units ÷ 30 staff = about 733 units per worker. If productivity improves as the skills gap closes, the rise is affordable; if defects at 3.5% persist, unit labour cost rises and the $15.00 contribution per unit is squeezed.

Polysilicon and glass inputs (13.5%): SOL's variable cost of $15.00 per unit will be affected, but the insert does not decompose it, so only a bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 13.5% it would add 13.5% × $15.00 = $2.03 per unit, and at 22,000 units that is about $44,600 a year (22,000 × $2.03). Even a smaller pass-through cuts the $15.00 contribution materially. SOL can offset part through the $1.00 warranty premium in the survey.

Conclusion: The 13.5% polysilicon and glass rise will have the greatest impact because it compounds across all 22,000 units and directly erodes the $15.00 contribution that supports the $1,200,000 line. The wage rise is second because it can be managed through productivity; the interest-rate effect is smallest and can be fixed. SOL should secure the $1.00 premium and seek cheaper certified inputs to protect margins.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to SOL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on SOL's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of SOL with a well-justified judgment that input costs have the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
